topics.name: Seafloor spreading
topics.kicker: New ocean crust forms at mid-ocean ridges · Proposed by Harry Hess
topics.briefing: Down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean runs an undersea mountain range where the ocean floor is splitting apart. Magma rises into the crack, cools into new rock, and slowly pushes older rock away on both sides, like two conveyor belts. Harry Hess proposed this idea around 1960, and stripes of magnetized rock on the seafloor soon backed it up, explaining how continents can drift apart.
topics.answerHtml: Seafloor spreading (accept sea-floor spreading or ocean-floor spreading; prompt on spreading or divergent boundaries; do not accept “continental drift” or “plate tectonics”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: While commanding the USS _Cape Johnson_ in World War II, a geologist used the ship’s echo sounder to map the Pacific floor and named flat-topped undersea mountains guyots [“GHEE-ohz”]. That geologist later proposed this process in a paper he called “an essay in geopoetry.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, described by Harry Hess, in which new oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves outward.

tossups.p: Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews supported this process in 1963 by explaining matching stripes of rock magnetized in opposite directions on both sides of an undersea ridge. Lawrence Morley reached the same idea independently. Those stripes formed because Earth’s magnetic field flips every so often.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, proposed by Harry Hess, in which new ocean crust forms at mid-ocean ridges.

tossups.p: Cores drilled by the research ship _Glomar Challenger_ in the late 1960s helped confirm this process. They showed that the oldest sediment resting on the ocean crust gets older farther from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which magma rising at mid-ocean ridges creates new crust that moves outward on both sides.

tossups.p: Robert Dietz coined the name of this process in a 1961 paper. In Iceland, visitors can walk through the Thingvellir [“THING-vet-leer”] rift valley, one of the few places on land where this process happens.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, proposed by Harry Hess, that creates new oceanic crust at divergent plate boundaries.

tossups.p: While drawing maps of the ocean floor with Bruce Heezen, Marie Tharp noticed a deep rift valley running down the center of an undersea mountain range. That rift valley marks where this process creates new crust along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process by which new ocean crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and slowly moves away from them.

tossups.p: J. Tuzo Wilson named the transform faults that cut across and offset the undersea ridges where this process happens. Those ridges, like the fast-opening East Pacific Rise, are divergent boundaries where magma wells up between two plates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, described by Harry Hess, that creates new oceanic crust.

tossups.p: As new rock made by this process cools, tiny grains of magnetite pass their Curie [“KYOOR-ee”] point and lock in the direction of Earth’s magnetic field. Because that field flips every so often, the ocean floor records the flips as matching stripes on either side of a ridge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves outward like a conveyor belt.

tossups.p: In 1977, the submersible _Alvin_ discovered hydrothermal vents teeming with life near the Galápagos Islands, along a crack where this process occurs. Black smokers, chimneys that spew hot, mineral-rich water, are also found where this process makes new crust.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, first proposed by Harry Hess, in which magma rises at mid-ocean ridges to form new ocean floor.

tossups.p: Ophiolites [“OH-fee-uh-lites”], like those found in Oman and Cyprus, are slices of ocean crust made by this process that were later pushed up onto land. Rounded pillow lavas form when magma erupts underwater during this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which new oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves away from them.

tossups.p: This process runs several times faster at the East Pacific Rise than at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where it widens the ocean by only a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Because of it, North America and Europe are slowly moving apart.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, proposed by Harry Hess, that creates new crust at mid-ocean ridges.

tossups.p: The plate motions behind this process are thought to be driven partly by “ridge push” and by “slab pull,” as old, cold crust sinks into the mantle at deep-ocean trenches. Because subduction destroys old crust about as fast as this process makes new crust, Earth does not grow larger.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which new oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves outward on both sides.

tossups.p: Heat flowing out of the ocean floor is greatest where this process occurs, and the blanket of sediment covering the ocean floor gets thicker moving away from those places. That is because the crust there is youngest and has had the least time to cool and collect sediment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, proposed by Harry Hess, in which new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges.

tossups.p: This process is slowly widening the Red Sea, which could one day become a full ocean as the Arabian Peninsula pulls away from Africa. The same process opened the Atlantic Ocean after the supercontinent Pangaea broke apart.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, proposed by Harry Hess, that forms new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges.

tossups.p: This process finally gave a mechanism for Alfred Wegener’s idea of continental drift, which many scientists had rejected because Wegener could not explain what moved the continents. Together, these ideas grew into the theory of plate tectonics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, described by Harry Hess, in which new ocean crust forms at mid-ocean ridges.

tossups.p: Rocks on the ocean floor get older the farther they are from an undersea mountain range, with matching patterns on both sides. This process explains why the ocean floor is so much younger than most of the rock on the continents.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which magma rising at mid-ocean ridges creates new crust that moves outward.

clues.t: New oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves outward on both sides
Proposed by Princeton geologist Harry Hess in the early 1960s
Happens at divergent boundaries, where two plates pull apart
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the classic example, slowly widening the Atlantic Ocean
Magma rises into the crack, cools into new rock, and moves away like a conveyor belt
Matching stripes of normal and reversed magnetism lie on both sides of a ridge, because Earth’s magnetic field flips
Ocean-floor rock gets older moving away from a ridge, so the ocean floor is far younger than most continental rock
Gave a mechanism for Alfred Wegener’s continental drift and helped build the theory of plate tectonics
Old crust is recycled into the mantle at deep-ocean trenches by subduction, so Earth does not grow larger
Marie Tharp found the rift valley down the middle of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge while mapping the ocean floor with Bruce Heezen
Sediment gets thicker and heat flow gets lower moving away from a ridge
Fastest at the East Pacific Rise; slow at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, about as fast as fingernails grow
Underwater eruptions at the ridges form rounded pillow lavas made of basalt
It is slowly widening the Red Sea, and it opened the Atlantic after Pangaea broke apart
Hess called his 1962 paper “History of Ocean Basins” “an essay in geopoetry”
Robert Dietz coined its name in a 1961 paper
Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews (1963), and Lawrence Morley on his own, explained the magnetic stripes with it
Drilling by the research ship _Glomar Challenger_ in the late 1960s helped confirm it
Magnetite grains lock in the direction of Earth’s field as new rock cools past their Curie point
Hess used the echo sounder of the USS _Cape Johnson_ in World War II and named flat-topped undersea mountains guyots
J. Tuzo Wilson named the transform faults that cut across and offset the ridges
In 1977 the submersible _Alvin_ found hydrothermal vents near the Galápagos; black smokers also form along the ridges
Ophiolites, like those in Oman and Cyprus, are slices of ocean crust it made that were pushed up onto land
“Ridge push” and “slab pull” help drive the plate motions behind it
Iceland’s Thingvellir rift valley is one of the few places where it happens on land

trap.title: Not drift, not the ridge
trap.body: Three neighboring answers trip players up. Continental drift was Alfred Wegener’s older idea that the continents move; plate tectonics is the big theory that ties everything together; and the mid-ocean ridge is the place where this process happens. Clues about Harry Hess, magnetic stripes, and new crust forming want seafloor spreading, so answering any of the other three loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Wegener, Pangaea, matching fossils, and puzzle-piece coastlines mean continental drift. Rigid plates and all three kinds of boundaries mean plate tectonics. Harry Hess, magnetic stripes, rocks getting older away from a ridge, and new ocean crust mean seafloor spreading; saying only “spreading” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Seafloor spreading (accept sea-floor spreading; prompt on spreading or divergent boundaries; do not accept “continental drift” or “plate tectonics”)

topics.name: Feldspar
topics.kicker: Most abundant mineral group in Earth’s crust · Weathers into clay
topics.dates: Orthoclase marks 6 on the Mohs scale
topics.briefing: Feldspars are the most common minerals in Earth’s crust, found in many kinds of rock, from granite to basalt. The name comes from German words meaning “field spar,” and the pink grains in some granite countertops are usually feldspar. Over time, rain slowly breaks these minerals down into clay, so the mud of a riverbank and the porcelain in a teacup may both have started out as feldspar.
topics.answerHtml: Feldspars (accept specific types such as alkali feldspar, potassium feldspar, or plagioclase feldspar; prompt on silicates; do not accept “quartz” or “mica”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Florida made moonstone its state gem to honor the Moon landings, even though moonstone is not found naturally there, and Oregon chose sunstone. Both gems are varieties of this group of minerals, whose potassium-rich members give some granite a pink color.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most abundant mineral group in Earth’s crust, which includes orthoclase and plagioclase.

tossups.p: The bright highlands of the Moon are made largely of anorthosite [“an-OR-thuh-site”], a rock made almost entirely of one kind of this mineral group. That kind forms a series that runs from sodium-rich albite to calcium-rich anorthite.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of minerals, the most abundant in Earth’s crust, that includes plagioclase and orthoclase.

tossups.p: One member of this mineral group is named for Greek words meaning “straight break,” because its two cleavage planes meet at a right angle, while another member’s name means “oblique break.” Friedrich Mohs chose that first member to mark a hardness of 6 on his scale.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mineral group whose name comes from German words for “field” and “spar.”

tossups.p: A sandstone rich in grains of this mineral group is called arkose [“AR-kohs”]. Chemical weathering by water slowly breaks this mineral group down into clays such as kaolinite [“KAY-uh-lih-nite”], which potters use to make porcelain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most abundant mineral group in Earth’s crust, which includes orthoclase and plagioclase.

tossups.p: Fine, parallel grooves called striations, caused by repeated twinning of the crystals, help geologists tell one series of this mineral group from the other. Carlsbad twins are common in this group’s potassium-rich members.
tossups.r: Its sodium- and calcium-rich members are called plagioclase. For 10 points, name this most abundant mineral group in Earth’s crust.

tossups.p: In Bowen’s reaction series, the continuous branch is made up of this group’s calcium- and sodium-bearing members, which change from calcium-rich to sodium-rich as magma cools. Its potassium-rich members crystallize near the end of the series, along with muscovite and quartz.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most abundant mineral group in Earth’s crust, which includes orthoclase and plagioclase.

tossups.p: Crystals of sanidine [“SAN-ih-deen”], a high-temperature member of this group found in volcanic rocks, are often dated by measuring the argon that builds up as their potassium-40 decays. Microcline is another potassium-rich member of this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of minerals, the most common in Earth’s crust, whose members include orthoclase and plagioclase.

tossups.p: Minerals such as nepheline [“NEF-uh-leen”] and leucite [“LOO-site”] form instead of this mineral group when a magma has too little silica. This group’s common members are aluminum silicates that also contain potassium, sodium, or calcium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of minerals that includes orthoclase and plagioclase and makes up much of granite.

tossups.p: Graphic granite shows wedge-shaped quartz crystals growing inside a single crystal of this mineral group, looking like ancient cuneiform writing. Pegmatites, extremely coarse-grained igneous rocks, can hold giant crystals of this mineral group alongside quartz and mica.
tossups.r: With quartz, it makes up most of granite. For 10 points, name this mineral group, including orthoclase and plagioclase.

tossups.p: Most of this mineral group that is mined ends up in glass and ceramics, where it works as a flux that helps the other ingredients melt at lower temperatures. Its crystals are hard enough to scratch glass and split along two cleavage planes at nearly right angles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most abundant mineral group in Earth’s crust, which includes orthoclase and plagioclase.

tossups.p: Perthite forms when a crystal of this mineral group separates into thin, alternating layers of sodium-rich and potassium-rich material as it cools. Amazonite, a blue-green gem, is a variety of this group’s potassium-rich member microcline.
tossups.r: This group also includes orthoclase and plagioclase. For 10 points, name this most abundant mineral group in Earth’s crust.

tossups.p: Labradorite [“LAB-ruh-dor-ite”], named for a region of Canada, is a member of this mineral group that flashes blue, green, and gold in a play of color called labradorescence. Sunstone, another gem from this group, sparkles because of tiny flakes of copper or hematite trapped inside it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mineral group, the most common in Earth’s crust, that includes plagioclase and orthoclase.

tossups.p: Like quartz, this mineral group is a framework silicate, in which every silicon–oxygen tetrahedron shares all four corners with its neighbors, but in this group some of the silicon is replaced by aluminum.
tossups.r: Its members include orthoclase and plagioclase. For 10 points, name this most abundant mineral group in Earth’s crust.

tossups.p: Light bouncing between microscopic layers inside moonstone gives it a soft, glowing sheen called adularescence [“ad-yoo-luh-RESS-unss”]. Those layers are made of two different minerals from this group, one rich in potassium and one rich in sodium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mineral group, the most abundant in Earth’s crust, which includes orthoclase and plagioclase.

tossups.p: These minerals make up more of Earth’s crust than any other mineral group, and with quartz they form most of the grains in granite. They come in two main series: potassium-rich alkali types and sodium- and calcium-rich plagioclase types.
tossups.r: One member, orthoclase, marks 6 on the Mohs hardness scale. For 10 points, name this mineral group.

clues.t: The most abundant group of minerals in Earth’s crust
Two main kinds: potassium-rich alkali types, like orthoclase, and sodium- and calcium-rich plagioclase types
With quartz, it makes up most of granite; its potassium-rich crystals can make granite pink
Orthoclase marks a hardness of 6 on the Mohs scale
Its name comes from German words meaning “field” and “spar”
Silicates containing aluminum plus potassium, sodium, or calcium
Splits along two good cleavage planes at nearly right angles, and is hard enough to scratch glass
In Greek, orthoclase means “straight break” and plagioclase means “oblique break”
The plagioclase series runs from sodium-rich albite to calcium-rich anorthite
Chemical weathering turns it into clays like kaolinite, used to make porcelain
Plagioclase crystals show fine, parallel striations caused by repeated twinning
Moonstone (Florida’s state gem) and sunstone (Oregon’s state gem), which sparkles with tiny copper or hematite flakes, are varieties of it
Labradorite, named for a region of Canada, flashes blue and green in a play of color called labradorescence
Mined mostly for glass and ceramics, where it acts as a flux that lowers melting temperatures
In Bowen’s reaction series, plagioclase forms the continuous branch; potassium-rich types crystallize near the end with muscovite and quartz
Anorthosite, made almost entirely of plagioclase, forms the Moon’s bright highlands
Like quartz, it is a framework silicate (tectosilicate), but with aluminum replacing some of the silicon
Sanidine crystals from volcanic rocks are dated by measuring argon made by potassium-40 decay
Nepheline and leucite form instead of it when a magma has too little silica
Perthite: a crystal that separated into thin sodium-rich and potassium-rich layers as it cooled
Carlsbad twins are common in its potassium-rich types
Arkose is a sandstone rich in its grains
Amazonite is a blue-green variety of microcline, one of its potassium-rich members
Graphic granite has quartz wedges inside one of its crystals, like cuneiform writing; pegmatites hold giant crystals of it
Moonstone’s glowing sheen, adularescence, comes from light scattering between thin layers of two of its kinds

trap.title: The group, not a member
trap.body: Tossups on this mineral group are packed with member names (orthoclase, plagioclase, microcline, albite, labradorite) and gems like moonstone, which tempts players to buzz with one of them. The question wants the whole family. Quartz is the other trap: it sits right beside this group in granite and is the second most abundant mineral in the crust.
trap.fix: Listen for “this group” or “these minerals,” and answer with the family name. A type that includes the family name, like “plagioclase feldspar,” is fine, but “plagioclase” alone is a different answer. Glassy, no cleavage, and hardness 7 mean quartz; two cleavage planes, hardness 6, and weathering into clay mean feldspar.
trap.line: Real answer line: Feldspars (accept specific types such as plagioclase feldspar or alkali feldspar; prompt on silicates; do not accept “quartz”)

topics.name: Moraines
topics.kicker: Ridges of rock debris dropped by glaciers · Mark where the ice once reached
topics.dates: Many formed during the last ice age
topics.briefing: When a glacier melts back, it drops everything it was carrying: a jumbled mix of boulders, gravel, sand, and clay called till. Those piles of debris are moraines, and they work like a glacier’s footprints, marking the sides of its path and the farthest point it reached. Long Island and Cape Cod are built partly from moraines left by the giant ice sheet that covered much of North America during the last ice age.
topics.answerHtml: Moraines (accept terminal, end, lateral, medial, recessional, or ground moraines; prompt on glacial deposits; do not accept “till,” “drumlins,” or “eskers”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The southern ends of New York’s Finger Lakes are blocked by the Valley Heads example of these landforms, which formed along the edge of a melting ice sheet. Bumpy ridges of this kind are made of an unsorted mix of boulders, gravel, sand, and clay called till.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ridges of rock debris deposited by glaciers, whose types include terminal and lateral.

tossups.p: Long Island’s “backbone” is made of two of these landforms, the Ronkonkoma [“ron-KONK-uh-muh”] and the Harbor Hill, left behind by the Laurentide Ice Sheet. Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket also formed partly from these deposits.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these piles of rock debris that glaciers drop at their edges, including the terminal kind that marks a glacier’s farthest advance.

tossups.p: Louis Agassiz [“AG-uh-see”] argued that a great ice age once covered much of Europe, pointing to these landforms and to giant boulders called erratics lying far from any modern glacier. He later found similar evidence in North America after moving to Harvard.
tossups.r: The terminal kind marks a glacier’s farthest advance. For 10 points, name these ridges of unsorted rock debris left by glaciers.

tossups.p: When two valley glaciers flow together, the debris along their touching edges joins into a single dark stripe running down the middle of the combined glacier, called the medial type of these features.
tossups.r: Lateral ones run along the sides of a glacier. For 10 points, name these ridges of rock debris, or till, left by glaciers.

tossups.p: In the Himalayas, lakes of meltwater held back by these landforms can burst through them, causing sudden, dangerous floods called glacial lake outburst floods. Such lakes often form behind the terminal type of these ridges as a glacier shrinks.
tossups.r: These landforms are made of unsorted sediment. For 10 points, name these ridges of rock debris, or till, deposited by glaciers.

tossups.p: Gently rolling till plains, like those across much of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, are made of the “ground” type of these deposits, which a glacier lays down in a sheet beneath itself.
tossups.r: The terminal type of these landforms marks the farthest point a glacier reached. For 10 points, name these deposits of glacial debris.

tossups.p: Each recessional example of these landforms marks a spot where a retreating glacier paused long enough to drop a new ridge of debris. Pits called kettles, often filled with water, dot many of their bumpy surfaces.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these piles of till left by glaciers, including the terminal kind that marks a glacier’s farthest advance.

tossups.p: Unlike the neatly sorted, layered sand and gravel of an outwash plain, these landforms are made of an unsorted jumble of boulders, gravel, sand, and clay dropped straight from glacier ice. That jumbled sediment is called till.
tossups.r: Their types include terminal, lateral, and medial. For 10 points, name these ridges of glacial debris.

tossups.p: In Wisconsin, a long, hilly example of these landforms that formed between two lobes of an ice sheet is dotted with kettle lakes and gives its name to a state forest. Geologists call that kind interlobate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ridges of till deposited by glaciers, whose lateral types form along a glacier’s sides.

tossups.p: The Valparaiso [“val-puh-RAY-zoh”] example of these landforms curves around the southern end of Lake Michigan, marking where a lobe of ice once stood. Like others of its kind, it is made of unsorted sediment called till.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ridges of rock debris left by glaciers, including terminal ones that mark a glacier’s farthest advance.

tossups.p: Rock debris riding on top of a glacier, called supraglacial debris, can pile up into these landforms when the ice beneath it melts. Rockfalls from valley walls feed the lateral type of these ridges, which line a glacier’s sides.
tossups.r: The terminal type marks a glacier’s farthest advance. For 10 points, name these ridges of till left behind by glaciers.

tossups.p: When a glacier advances, it can bulldoze loose sediment in front of it like a giant plow, building the “push” type of these landforms. Other kinds form when the ice simply melts and drops the debris it was carrying.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ridges of glacial till whose types include terminal, lateral, and medial.

tossups.p: Knob-and-kettle topography, a bumpy landscape of small hills and water-filled hollows, is common on the hummocky [“HUM-uh-kee”] type of these landforms, where buried blocks of ice melted long after the glacier retreated. Many of these landforms in the northern United States formed at the end of the last ice age.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ridges of unsorted rock debris dropped by glaciers, such as terminal and recessional ones.

tossups.p: Ancient rocks called tillites, the hardened remains of the jumbled sediment that makes up these landforms, helped Alfred Wegener argue that Africa, South America, India, and Australia were once joined near the South Pole.
tossups.r: Their types include terminal and lateral. For 10 points, name these ridges of till deposited by glaciers.

tossups.p: Scientists can estimate the age of a young example of these landforms by measuring how large the lichens on its boulders have grown, a method called lichenometry [“ly-kuh-NOM-uh-tree”]. The recessional type marks where a shrinking glacier paused.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these ridges of rock debris, or till, deposited at the edges of glaciers.

clues.t: Ridges or mounds of rock debris deposited by a glacier
Made of till: an unsorted mix of boulders, gravel, sand, and clay dropped by the ice
Types include terminal (or end), lateral, medial, recessional, and ground
The terminal kind marks the farthest point a glacier advanced
Long Island, Cape Cod, Martha’s Vineyard, and Nantucket formed partly from them
Lateral ones line a valley glacier’s sides, fed by rockfalls from the valley walls
Where two glaciers join, two lateral ones merge into a dark medial stripe down the middle
Recessional ones mark places where a retreating glacier paused
Ground ones are sheets of till laid down beneath a glacier, forming till plains like those of Ohio and Indiana
Unlike outwash plains, which meltwater sorts into layers, they are unsorted
Buried blocks of ice melt to leave kettles, pits that often fill with water
Many in North America were left by the Laurentide Ice Sheet during the last ice age
Meltwater lakes dammed behind them can burst out in glacial lake outburst floods
Glacial erratics, boulders carried far from where they formed, are often found with them
The Valley Heads example blocks the southern ends of New York’s Finger Lakes
Long Island’s two big ones are the Ronkonkoma and the Harbor Hill
Louis Agassiz used them and erratic boulders as evidence of a past ice age
Wisconsin’s interlobate example, formed between two lobes of ice and dotted with kettle lakes, names a state forest
The Valparaiso example curves around the southern end of Lake Michigan
Supraglacial debris riding on top of a glacier can pile up into them as the ice melts
An advancing glacier bulldozes loose sediment into “push” ones
Hummocky ones show knob-and-kettle topography of small hills and water-filled hollows
Tillite is hardened till; ancient tillites helped Alfred Wegener argue that the southern continents were once joined
Lichenometry dates young ones by measuring the lichens growing on their boulders

trap.title: Moraine, till, or drumlin?
trap.body: Glacier tossups name a whole family of deposits, and players often grab the wrong one. Till is the jumbled sediment itself, not the landform built from it. Drumlins are smooth, egg-shaped hills shaped beneath moving ice, eskers are snaking ridges of sand and gravel left by meltwater streams, and erratics are single boulders carried far from home.
trap.fix: If the clue says “terminal,” “lateral,” “medial,” or “recessional,” or describes a ridge marking a glacier’s edge or farthest advance, answer moraines. Save “till” for questions about the unsorted sediment and “glaciers” for questions about the moving ice itself.
trap.line: Real answer line: Moraines (accept specific types like terminal or lateral moraines; prompt on glacial deposits; do not accept “till”)

topics.name: Tides
topics.kicker: Twice-daily rise and fall of the sea · Driven mostly by the Moon’s gravity
topics.dates: High water about every 12 hours 25 minutes
topics.briefing: Twice a day, along most coasts, the ocean creeps up the beach and then slides back out again. These tides happen because the Moon’s gravity pulls a little harder on the side of Earth facing it, stretching the oceans into two bulges that Earth spins through. In Canada’s Bay of Fundy, the difference between high and low tide is the greatest in the world, enough to leave boats sitting on the mud.
topics.answerHtml: Tides (accept tidal forces; accept spring or neap tides; prompt on sea level changes; do not accept “tidal waves,” “waves,” or “currents”)
prompt: rise and fall of the sea

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Galileo wrongly argued that these events were caused by Earth’s spin and its motion around the Sun, and he used them as evidence that Earth moves. Isaac Newton correctly explained them in his _Principia_ as an effect of gravity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these twice-daily rises and falls of sea level caused mostly by the Moon.

tossups.p: In most ocean basins, these events rotate around amphidromic [“am-fih-DROH-mik”] points, where the water barely rises or falls at all. Lines linking places where these events peak at the same time radiate outward from those points like the spokes of a wheel.
tossups.r: Their range is greatest in Canada’s Bay of Fundy. For 10 points, name these daily rises and falls of the ocean.

tossups.p: Friction from these events is slowly lengthening Earth’s day and pushing the Moon about 3.8 centimeters farther away each year, a change measured by bouncing lasers off mirrors left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts.
tossups.r: Most coasts get two high and two low ones each day. For 10 points, name these rises and falls of the ocean caused mainly by the Moon’s gravity.

tossups.p: Lord Kelvin built the first machine to predict these events, using a system of pulleys and gears to add up the many separate cycles that make them up. Their two daily highs are usually about 12 hours and 25 minutes apart.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rises and falls of sea level caused by the gravity of the Moon and Sun.

tossups.p: Pierre-Simon Laplace [“luh-PLAHS”] wrote equations that treat these events as huge, slow waves moving through the ocean, instead of as fixed bulges of water. That improved on an earlier explanation by Isaac Newton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these daily rises and falls of sea level, which are largest in the Bay of Fundy.

tossups.p: Even though the Sun’s gravity on Earth is far stronger than the Moon’s, the Sun produces less than half as much of these, because they depend on how much a pull changes from one side of Earth to the other, which shrinks with the cube of distance.
tossups.r: When the Sun and Moon line up, their spring type is extra strong. For 10 points, name these twice-daily rises and falls of the sea.

tossups.p: The spring type of these, which has nothing to do with the season, happens near new and full moon, when the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up. The neap type, with the smallest range, happens near the quarter moons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these daily rises and falls of the ocean caused by the Moon’s pull.

tossups.p: China’s Qiantang [“chyen-TAHNG”] River and England’s Severn are famous for bores, walls of water that rush upstream when these events push seawater into a narrowing river mouth. The Amazon’s version is called the pororoca [“por-oh-ROH-kuh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these twice-daily rises and falls of sea level, which are greatest in Canada’s Bay of Fundy.

tossups.p: Jupiter’s pull squeezes and stretches its moon Io, heating its interior enough to power hundreds of volcanoes, in a process named for these events. The same kind of flexing may keep an ocean liquid under Europa’s ice.
tossups.r: On Earth, these are caused mostly by the Moon. For 10 points, name these regular rises and falls of the ocean.

tossups.p: France’s La Rance power station has used these events to make electricity since 1966, letting water flow through turbines in a dam across an estuary. Not far away, Mont-Saint-Michel can become an island when these events flood the sands around it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these daily rises and falls of sea level caused by the Moon’s gravity.

tossups.p: California grunion fish swim onto beaches at night to lay their eggs in the sand just after the highest of these events. In the zone between the high and low water marks, these events leave behind pools full of sea stars and crabs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rises and falls of the sea caused by the Moon and Sun.

tossups.p: Sailors call the falling stage of these events the ebb and the rising stage the flood, with a brief pause called slack water in between. Printed tables list the times of these events for each day of the year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these twice-daily rises and falls of sea level caused mainly by the Moon.

tossups.p: These events come from two bulges of water, one on the side of Earth facing the Moon and one on the opposite side, which Earth spins through each day. That is why most coasts get two highs and two lows daily.
tossups.r: Their greatest range is in the Bay of Fundy. For 10 points, name these regular rises and falls of the ocean.

tossups.p: Long ago, the same kind of stretching force behind these events slowed the Moon’s spin until it always kept one face toward Earth. Inside a planet’s Roche [“ROHSH”] limit, that force can tear a moon apart.
tossups.r: On Earth, this force makes the oceans bulge toward and away from the Moon. For 10 points, name these twice-daily rises and falls of sea level.

tossups.p: The solid ground under your feet also rises and falls slightly twice a day in a rocky version of these events, too gently for anyone to feel. In the ocean, the difference between their high and low water levels is called their range.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rises and falls of sea level caused mostly by the Moon’s gravity.

clues.t: The regular rise and fall of sea level, usually twice a day
Caused mainly by the Moon’s gravity, with help from the Sun
Canada’s Bay of Fundy has the greatest range in the world
Spring ones (biggest range) come near new and full moon; neap ones (smallest range) near the quarter moons
Most coasts get two highs and two lows each day
The Moon’s uneven pull stretches the oceans into two bulges: one facing the Moon and one on the far side
Highs come about every 12 hours 25 minutes, so they arrive about 50 minutes later each day
The falling stage is the ebb, the rising stage is the flood, and the pause in between is slack water
Isaac Newton first explained them with gravity in his _Principia_
Bores, walls of water rushing upriver, form on China’s Qiantang, England’s Severn, and the Amazon (where it is called the pororoca)
The height difference between high and low water is called the range
France’s La Rance station (since 1966) and South Korea’s Sihwa Lake station make electricity from them
The Sun’s effect is less than half the Moon’s, because this stretching weakens with the cube of distance
The zone between the high and low water marks holds pools full of sea stars and crabs
Galileo wrongly blamed them on Earth’s spin and orbit and used them as evidence that Earth moves
They rotate around amphidromic points, where the water barely rises or falls
Pierre-Simon Laplace’s equations treat them as huge, slow waves instead of fixed bulges
Lord Kelvin built the first machine to predict them, using pulleys and gears
Their friction lengthens Earth’s day and pushes the Moon away about 3.8 cm a year, measured with lasers and Apollo mirrors
The same stretching force slowed the Moon’s spin until one face always points toward Earth
Inside a planet’s Roche limit, this stretching force can tear a moon apart
Jupiter’s squeezing heats Io enough to power its volcanoes and may keep Europa’s ocean liquid
California grunion lay their eggs on beaches at night just after the highest ones
Mont-Saint-Michel in France can become an island when they flood the surrounding sands
Solid ground also rises and falls slightly twice a day in a rocky version of them
The biggest spring ones, when the Moon is also closest to Earth, are nicknamed “king” ones

trap.title: Not waves, not tsunamis
trap.body: A tsunami is sometimes called a “tidal wave,” but it has nothing to do with these: tsunamis come from earthquakes, landslides, or eruptions. Red tides are blooms of algae, and rip currents (often called “rip tides”) are narrow streams of water flowing away from the beach. Their names sound right, so a quick buzz on any of them loses the tossup.
trap.fix: If the clues mention the Moon and Sun lining up, spring and neap, the Bay of Fundy, or highs about 12 hours apart, answer tides. Wind makes ordinary waves, earthquakes make tsunamis, and algae make red tides.
trap.line: Real answer line: Tides (accept tidal forces; accept spring tides or neap tides; do not accept “tidal waves” or “tsunamis”)

topics.name: Aquifers
topics.kicker: Rock layers that store groundwater · Tapped by wells for drinking and farms
topics.dates: Hold most of Earth’s liquid fresh water
topics.briefing: An aquifer is a layer of underground rock or sediment, like sand, gravel, or cracked limestone, that soaks up water like a sponge and lets it flow through. People drill wells into aquifers to get water for drinking and farming. The giant Ogallala Aquifer under the Great Plains waters crops in eight states, but in many places farmers are pumping it out faster than rain can refill it.
topics.answerHtml: Aquifers (accept confined, unconfined, or artesian aquifers; prompt on groundwater; do not accept “water table” or “aquitard”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Henry Darcy’s law, which he published in an 1856 report on the public fountains of Dijon [“dee-ZHOHN”], France, describes how water flows through these underground layers. Darcy found that the flow depends on how steeply the water level drops and how easily water passes through the material.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these layers of porous rock or sediment that store groundwater, such as the Ogallala.

tossups.p: One type of these layers gets its name from the French region of Artois [“ar-TWAH”], where people long ago drilled wells in which water rose to the surface on its own. That confined type is trapped under pressure between watertight layers called aquicludes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underground layers of rock or sediment that hold groundwater and supply wells.

tossups.p: According to the Ghyben–Herzberg relation, fresh water in these layers beneath an ocean island floats on denser seawater and reaches about 40 times deeper below sea level than the water table rises above it. Pumping too much from them can pull in salt water.
tossups.r: Wells are drilled into them to reach water. For 10 points, name these underground layers of permeable rock that hold groundwater.

tossups.p: Libya’s Great Man-Made River pipes ancient “fossil water” to coastal cities from the Nubian Sandstone system of these formations, which lies beneath the Sahara. Much of that water soaked in thousands of years ago, when the region was far wetter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underground layers of rock or sediment that store groundwater and supply wells.

tossups.p: Center-pivot sprinklers have steadily lowered the water level in a huge one of these formations under the Great Plains, which stretches beneath parts of eight states from South Dakota to Texas. Farmers rely on it to grow corn, wheat, and cotton.
tossups.r: That one is the Ogallala. For 10 points, name these underground layers of rock or sediment that hold groundwater.

tossups.p: Comal Springs and San Marcos Springs bubble out of Texas’s Edwards example of these formations, whose cave-filled limestone is home to the endangered Texas blind salamander. The city of San Antonio gets much of its drinking water from it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underground layers of rock that hold groundwater and supply wells.

tossups.p: Pumping a well lowers the water level around it into a funnel shape called a cone of depression, which can dry up nearby shallow wells that tap the same one of these layers.
tossups.r: Unconfined ones have the water table as their top surface. For 10 points, name these underground layers of permeable rock or sediment that hold groundwater.

tossups.p: The Guarani [“gwah-rah-NEE”] system of these formations, named for an Indigenous people of South America, lies beneath parts of Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay. Its water is held in the tiny spaces between grains of sandstone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underground layers of rock or sediment from which wells draw groundwater.

tossups.p: A good example of these layers needs high porosity, meaning lots of open space between grains, and high permeability, meaning water can flow easily between those spaces. Clay has high porosity but such low permeability that it usually blocks water instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underground layers of rock or sediment, such as sand and gravel, that hold groundwater.

tossups.p: Parts of California’s San Joaquin [“san wah-KEEN”] Valley sank by several meters during the 1900s as farmers pumped water out of these layers and the drained clay squeezed together. Mexico City has also sunk for the same reason.
tossups.r: Wells are drilled into them. For 10 points, name these underground layers of permeable rock or sediment that hold groundwater.

tossups.p: Australia’s Great Artesian Basin, the world’s largest system of the confined type of these formations, lets ranchers in the dry Outback reach water through wells that Australians call bores. In many of those wells, water rises without any pumping.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underground layers of permeable rock or sediment that store groundwater and supply wells.

tossups.p: The Floridan [“FLOR-ih-dun”] system of these formations is made of limestone riddled with channels that water has dissolved, and it feeds Florida’s many large freshwater springs. Cities across Florida and southern Georgia draw drinking water from it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underground layers of rock that hold groundwater, which can be confined or unconfined.

tossups.p: Leaky layers called aquitards slow water moving between these formations, while aquicludes, often made of clay or shale, block it almost completely. Unconfined types of these formations are refilled by rain and snowmelt soaking straight down from the surface.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underground layers of porous rock or sediment that hold groundwater.

tossups.p: Below the vadose [“VAY-dohss”] zone, where soil pores hold both air and water, lies the saturated, or phreatic [“free-AT-ik”], zone, where these layers are found. The boundary between those two zones is called the water table.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underground layers of rock or sediment that wells tap for groundwater.

tossups.p: The name of these formations comes from Latin words meaning “water-bearing.” Rain and snowmelt refill them in places called recharge zones, and their water can flow back out at springs, rivers, and wetlands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these underground layers of porous rock or sediment, like the Ogallala, that hold groundwater.

clues.t: An underground layer of permeable rock or sediment that holds groundwater and lets it flow
People drill wells into them to get drinking water and water for irrigation
The Ogallala, or High Plains, one lies under the Great Plains in parts of eight states
Good ones are made of sand, gravel, sandstone, or cracked limestone
The top surface of an unconfined one is the water table
Confined ones are trapped under pressure; water can rise on its own in artesian wells, named for Artois, France
Aquitards slow water down, and aquicludes, such as clay or shale, nearly block it
They need high porosity (open space) and high permeability (how easily water flows); clay is porous but blocks water
Rain and snowmelt refill them in recharge zones; their water flows back out at springs, rivers, and wetlands
Pumping a well creates a funnel-shaped cone of depression in the water level around it
Overpumping can make the land sink, called subsidence, as in California’s San Joaquin Valley and Mexico City
Near coasts, overpumping can draw seawater in: saltwater intrusion
Center-pivot irrigation is draining the Ogallala faster than rain refills it in many places
Texas’s Edwards one, in cave-filled limestone, supplies San Antonio and is home to the endangered Texas blind salamander
Henry Darcy’s law, published in 1856 in a report on the public fountains of Dijon, France, describes how water flows through them
Libya’s Great Man-Made River pipes ancient “fossil water” from the Nubian Sandstone system under the Sahara
The Guarani system lies beneath Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay
Australia’s Great Artesian Basin is the world’s largest confined system; Outback wells there are called bores
The Floridan one is limestone full of channels dissolved by water, and it feeds Florida’s big springs
Ghyben–Herzberg relation: under an island, the freshwater lens reaches about 40 times deeper below sea level than the water table rises above it
Its name comes from Latin words meaning “water-bearing”
The unsaturated vadose zone lies above the water table; the saturated phreatic zone lies below it
Comal Springs and San Marcos Springs flow out of Texas’s Edwards one
Hydrogeology is the study of groundwater and the layers that hold it

trap.title: Layer, table, or well?
trap.body: The water table is not this answer: it is only the top surface of the saturated ground, the line where the water starts. A well is the hole people drill to reach the water, an aquitard or aquiclude is a layer that slows or blocks water, and groundwater is the water itself. This answer is the rock or sediment layer that holds the water and lets it flow.
trap.fix: If the clue describes a layer of sand, gravel, sandstone, or limestone that stores water and supplies wells, or names the Ogallala, Edwards, or Floridan, answer aquifers. “Groundwater” earns only a prompt, so be ready to name the layer.
trap.line: Real answer line: Aquifers (accept confined or artesian aquifers; prompt on groundwater; do not accept “water table” or “aquitard”)

topics.name: Stratosphere
topics.kicker: Second layer of the atmosphere · Home of the ozone layer
topics.dates: Roughly 10 to 50 km above the ground
topics.briefing: The stratosphere is the second layer of Earth’s atmosphere, starting about 10 kilometers up, above the clouds and storms of the troposphere. Strangely, it gets warmer as you go higher, because its ozone soaks up the Sun’s ultraviolet light, the same ozone layer that shields us from sunburn-causing rays. Jets cruise near its bottom edge, and in 2012 skydiver Felix Baumgartner jumped from a balloon high inside it.
topics.answerHtml: Stratosphere (prompt on atmosphere or upper atmosphere; do not accept “troposphere,” “mesosphere,” or “ozone layer”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Léon Teisserenc de Bort and Richard Assmann independently discovered this layer around 1902, after instrument-carrying balloons showed that air stops getting colder above a certain height. Teisserenc de Bort named it for the Latin word for “layer,” thinking its air did not mix.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere, above the troposphere, that contains the ozone layer.

tossups.p: High above the equator, the winds in this layer switch back and forth between blowing from the east and from the west in a cycle lasting about 28 months, called the quasi-biennial [“KWAY-zye bye-EN-ee-ul”] oscillation. Ozone in this layer absorbs ultraviolet light, so its temperature rises with height.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this second layer of Earth’s atmosphere, found between the troposphere and the mesosphere.

tossups.p: The slow Brewer–Dobson circulation lifts air into this layer over the tropics and carries it toward the poles, which is why ozone made over the tropics piles up at high latitudes. Gordon Dobson also gave his name to the unit used to measure ozone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere that contains the ozone layer, just above the troposphere.

tossups.p: In 1931, Auguste Piccard [“pee-KAR”] and Paul Kipfer became the first people to reach this layer, riding in a sealed, pressurized cabin hung beneath a giant balloon. Piccard later inspired the cartoon scientist Professor Calculus in _The Adventures of Tintin_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere, home to the ozone layer, that lies above the troposphere.

tossups.p: Shimmering nacreous [“NAY-kree-us”] clouds, also called “mother-of-pearl” clouds, can form in this layer over the poles during winter, and their icy particles help chlorine destroy ozone. That destruction creates the ozone hole that appears over Antarctica each spring.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this second layer of Earth’s atmosphere, where most ozone is found, just above the troposphere.

tossups.p: Sulfur gas blasted into this layer by the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo [“pin-uh-TOO-boh”] formed a haze of tiny droplets that cooled the whole planet for about two years. Because this layer has almost no rain or weather, such particles can linger there for a long time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere above the troposphere, home to the ozone layer.

tossups.p: In 2014, Alan Eustace set a record by skydiving from a balloon high in this layer, beating the height of Felix Baumgartner’s 2012 jump, in which Baumgartner broke the sound barrier in free fall. Weather balloons often rise through much of this layer before they burst.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere, between the troposphere and mesosphere, that holds the ozone layer.

tossups.p: Unlike the layer below it, this layer gets warmer the higher you go, because the ozone inside it absorbs the Sun’s ultraviolet light. That warm air on top makes this layer very stable, so its air barely mixes up and down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this second layer of Earth’s atmosphere, which contains the ozone layer.

tossups.p: Sydney Chapman explained in 1930 how ozone forms in this layer: ultraviolet light splits oxygen molecules into single atoms, which then join other oxygen molecules to make ozone. About 90 percent of Earth’s ozone is found in this layer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere that lies just above the troposphere.

tossups.p: In 1985, Joseph Farman’s team at the British Antarctic Survey reported that ozone in this layer was thinning sharply over Antarctica each spring. Two years later, the Montreal Protocol was signed to phase out the CFC chemicals responsible.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere above the troposphere, where the ozone layer is found.

tossups.p: The supersonic Concorde airliner cruised in this layer, about 18 kilometers up, high above nearly all clouds and storms, and the U-2 spy plane has flown even higher in it. Many ordinary jets fly near its bottom edge, where the air is smooth and thin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere that contains the ozone layer, just above the troposphere.

tossups.p: This layer ends about 50 kilometers up, at a boundary where temperatures stop rising and the mesosphere begins. Its lower boundary, the tropopause, is higher over the equator than over the poles.
tossups.r: It sits directly above the troposphere, where weather happens. For 10 points, name this layer of Earth’s atmosphere that contains the ozone layer.

tossups.p: Sudden warmings in this layer over the Arctic can weaken or split the polar vortex, sometimes sending frigid air south weeks later. Unlike the layer beneath it, this layer has very little water vapor, so clouds rarely form there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere that holds most of Earth’s ozone.

tossups.p: The flat, spreading anvil tops of big thunderstorms form when rising air hits the bottom of this layer and stops, because the air above it is warmer. The strongest storms can punch “overshooting tops” a short way into it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this second layer of Earth’s atmosphere, above the troposphere, that contains the ozone layer.

tossups.p: A thin haze of sulfuric acid droplets called the Junge [“YOONG-uh”] layer floats in this layer and grows thicker after big volcanic eruptions. Sulfur from Indonesia’s Mount Tambora reached this layer in 1815, leading to the “Year Without a Summer” in 1816.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere between the troposphere and mesosphere, home of the ozone layer.

clues.t: The second layer of the atmosphere, above the troposphere and below the mesosphere
Contains the ozone layer; about 90 percent of Earth’s ozone is found in it
Gets warmer with height, because its ozone absorbs the Sun’s ultraviolet light
Runs from roughly 10 kilometers up to about 50 kilometers up
Jets fly near its bottom edge, and the Concorde cruised in it, above nearly all weather
Its bottom boundary, the tropopause, is higher over the equator than over the poles
Named from the Latin for “layer,” because its stable air barely mixes up and down
CFCs thinned its ozone, creating the Antarctic ozone hole; the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased them out
Shimmering nacreous (“mother-of-pearl”) clouds form in it over the poles in winter and help chlorine destroy ozone
Very dry, with little water vapor, so clouds rarely form in it
Big eruptions like Mount Pinatubo’s in 1991 put sulfur into it, cooling Earth for about two years
Thunderstorm anvil tops flatten out when rising air hits its warmer bottom
Weather balloons rise through much of it before they burst
Felix Baumgartner (2012) and Alan Eustace (2014) skydived from balloons high in it
Discovered around 1902 by Léon Teisserenc de Bort and Richard Assmann, using instrument-carrying balloons
Auguste Piccard and Paul Kipfer first reached it in 1931 in a pressurized balloon cabin; Piccard inspired Tintin’s Professor Calculus
Its winds above the equator switch between easterly and westerly in a cycle of about 28 months: the quasi-biennial oscillation
The Brewer–Dobson circulation lifts air into it over the tropics and carries it toward the poles
Sydney Chapman (1930) explained how ultraviolet light makes ozone from oxygen in it
Joseph Farman’s British Antarctic Survey team reported the ozone hole in 1985
Sudden warmings in it can weaken or split the polar vortex, sending frigid air south
The Junge layer is a thin haze of sulfuric acid droplets inside it
Mount Tambora’s 1815 eruption sent sulfur into it, causing 1816’s “Year Without a Summer”
Ozone amounts are measured in Dobson units, named for Gordon Dobson
The U-2 spy plane has flown high in it, above the Concorde’s cruising height
Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson discovered the ozone layer inside it in 1913

trap.title: Which layer is which?
trap.body: The atmosphere’s layers have look-alike names, and quiz bowl asks about all of them. The troposphere is the bottom layer, where weather happens and temperature drops with height; the mesosphere sits above this one and is where most meteors burn up; and the ozone layer is only one part of this layer, not the whole thing. Saying “ozone layer” when the question wants the whole layer loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Remember the order going up: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere. Ozone, warming with height, jets, and weather balloons point to the stratosphere; weather and most clouds mean the troposphere; meteors and the coldest temperatures mean the mesosphere; auroras and the International Space Station mean the thermosphere.
trap.line: Real answer line: Stratosphere (prompt on atmosphere; do not accept “troposphere,” “mesosphere,” or “ozone layer”)
